source.title: A Unified Analysis of Mixed Sample Data Augmentation: A Loss Function Perspective
source.authors: Chanwoo Park; Sangdoo Yun; Sanghyuk Chun

record.file_problem: none; full paper text including appendices is supplied
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own results on whether mixed-sample augmentation changes generalization-related measures and validation accuracy, and refines the generalization account by showing that different mixing masks have task-dependent effects. It does not test memorization of random labels or most other claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's CIFAR-100 and ImageNet tables report validation accuracy for training methods that include Mixup, CutMix, HMix, and GMix; these results bear on V6 only insofar as the version concerns explicit regularization/data augmentation, and on V1 only as natural-label generalization under standard training if augmentation itself is the object. No random-label memorization, width sweep, architecture comparison, optimizer comparison, batch-size comparison, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or memorized-example removal test is reported. Figure 5/6 compare gradient products after Mixup and CutMix training. Cited results are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes mixed-sample data augmentation and compares augmentation methods. None of its results tests V1–V8. Augmentation comparisons do not test dropout or joint dropout/weight-decay removal in V6; input-gradient regularization and a theoretical first-layer flatness connection do not test the magnitude-aware sharpness correlation in V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors derive mask-dependent input-gradient, Hessian, and first-layer regularization connections under their assumptions, argue that mixing strategy should depend on the task, and propose HMix and GMix. They conclude that these methods outperform Mixup and CutMix and compare favorably with stochastic mixing on classification benchmarks, although individual table entries do not uniformly favor both proposed methods. Their generalization bounds do not test any listed claim version.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies mixed-sample data augmentation (Mixup, CutMix and proposed variants) and their theoretical regularization effects; it does not reproduce the methods or measures in the listed claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that optimal mixing strategy depends on application, dataset, architecture/model parameters, and pixel-level importance; large-crop versus small-crop scenarios reverse the Mixup/CutMix validation-accuracy ordering. Figure results state CutMix regularizes closer pixel gradient products more than Mixup.

fits_no_version.finding: CutMix exceeds Mixup by 6.1 percentage points under large crops but trails by 0.7 under small crops. ImageNet-1K accuracy rises from 75.68% without MSDA to 78.38% with HMix; CIFAR-100 results vary by architecture and augmentation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mixed-sample augmentation affects held-out classification accuracy, with relative performance depending on crop conditions, architecture, and mixing strategy.

fits_no_version.finding: Normalized partial input-gradient products differ by pixel distance after Mixup and CutMix training; CutMix more strongly suppresses nearby-pixel products.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mixing masks affect the spatial pattern of input-gradient regularization.

fits_no_version.finding: Augmentation rankings differ across occlusion, corruption, and adversarial evaluations: CutMix exceeds Mixup on occlusion accuracy, while Mixup exceeds CutMix on ImageNet-C.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mixed-sample augmentation changes robustness in ways that depend on the evaluation perturbation.

fits_no_version.finding: The paper derives an approximate loss decomposition and generalization bounds for restricted GLM and feature-level two-layer ReLU settings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under stated assumptions, mixed-sample augmentation induces regularization and bounds population loss through a constrained function class.

record.problems: Theoretical generalization claims are given as formal results under restricted assumptions, while the empirical classification tables report validation accuracy rather than train-test gaps. The reported CIFAR-100 averages across three runs but no uncertainty estimates are provided. Gradient-product comparisons are figure-only. The study does not test the claim's memorization premise or any of its listed versions directly.
record.rows_left_out: None; all extracted table and figure results kept (54 rows). Other robustness metrics for ImageNet-occ, ImageNet-C, and FGSM were retained because the table separately reports them; the paper itself treats these as robustness benchmarks, outside the claim's stated scope.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy alongside natural-label generalization using the same architectures and recipes.
Width-dependent test error beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout interventions, small-data and excessive-dropout regimes, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware weight sharpness versus generalization gaps and comparative rankings against norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All rows retain versions ["none"]. Their cannot_determine states concern applicability to V1–V8, not whether the reported accuracy differences are readable. Held-out accuracy can measure generalization, and error can be obtained from accuracy; the exclusion follows from the missing version-specific comparisons. ImageNet training explicitly uses weight decay 2×10^-5, batch size 512, and cosine scheduling (Appendix F). The record's claim that every table result was retained is inaccurate: Table 2 includes omitted architectures and Table 4 includes omitted HMix crop results, but none bears on V1–V8, so they do not warrant missing entries.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of random-label and natural-label test performance.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold test.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison.
No dropout intervention or comparison; mixed-sample augmentation is not dropout.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measure or ranking against norm- or margin-based measures.
No removal of memorized examples or test-accuracy comparison after their removal.
